phases.title:
Ship &
apply
phases.intro: Four weeks of finishing, not starting. The environment from Phase 3 gets hardened until a stranger can install it and reproduce your numbers; the work gets written up once, in three formats a reviewer will actually open; the code goes where the people who hire for this read code. Applications are not a Phase 4 activity — you started sending them in week 20 and this is the last checkpoint, not the first attempt.

callouts.html: Nothing new gets built in Phase 4. If the environment is not already running at the end of week 48, cut its scope instead of extending the timeline. A small environment that a stranger installed beats a large one nobody ran.
A reviewer gives you about 90 seconds. One link, one page, three artifacts above the fold, numbers with error bars. Everything you built in 52 weeks has to survive that budget or it does not exist.

items.title: Measure run-to-run variance before you touch anything else
items.desc: Run the full task suite at least five times against a fixed model and seed set, and record the spread per task, not just the mean. Decompose it: sampling noise from the model, nondeterminism in your verifier, flaky container startup, network timeouts. Report a number — "pass rate 0.62 ± 0.04 over 5 runs, n=120" — and name which source dominates. An environment whose numbers move and cannot say why is not usable by anyone.

items.title: Kill the nondeterminism you control
items.desc: Pin every version in the image, seed everything seedable, remove network calls from the verifier path, and make reset actually restore state rather than approximately restore it. Add a timeout and a retry policy with explicit accounting so a flaked sample is logged as flaked, not as failed. Re-measure variance after the fixes and report both numbers so the delta is visible.

items.title: Get a stranger to install it and use it
items.desc: Hand the repo to someone who has never seen it and watch them install it without helping. Every question they ask is a documentation bug — fix it rather than answering it. The exit condition is a person who is not you producing a run and a result they can interpret; until that happens you have a script, not an environment.

items.title: Claim a Prime Intellect environments bounty
items.desc: Prime Intellect pays $100–500 for open bounties and $1,000–5,000+ for application-only ones sponsored by third parties. Take one, even a small one. A paid bounty buys you three things a merged docs PR does not: a reviewer with an incentive to actually read your code, a named reference who can speak to your work, and money. It also forces your environment to meet an external spec instead of one you wrote for yourself.

callouts.html: Reliability is the deliverable, not the task. Anyone can write a task and a scorer in a weekend. The thing that is scarce — and the thing evals teams interview for — is knowing how much your own number moves and being able to say why.

items.title: The technical report — not a preprint
items.desc: Write a report as a markdown page or a plain HTML page in the repo: problem, method, setup, results with uncertainty, limitations, reproduction instructions. Do not put it on arXiv. A single-author unaffiliated non-peer-reviewed PDF reads as a warning sign more often than a signal, and the format costs you the one thing you need — a link a reviewer can skim in a browser tab without downloading anything.

items.title: The README that does the actual work
items.desc: Most reviewers never leave the README. First screen: what this is, what it measures, the headline number with its variance, install in three commands, one example run with real output. Limitations get their own section near the top, not an appendix. Link out to the technical report and the blog post from there.

items.title: One blog post with a point of view
items.desc: Write the post you would have wanted at week 35 — one specific thing you learned that is not in the docs. The benchmark discrepancy you found, the variance source that surprised you, what broke when a stranger installed your environment. Take a position and support it with your own numbers. Generic "my learning journey" posts convert to nothing; a post with a defensible claim gets cited and gets replies from people who hire.

callouts.html: Write the limitations section first. It is the fastest filter a reviewer has for whether you understand your own result, and drafting it early usually tells you which experiment you still need to run.

tasks.title: Contribute upstream and publish to the Hub

items.title: Land the contribution you have been building toward since week 4
items.desc: Substantive merged PRs follow months of presence in a community — triaging issues, answering questions, reviewing other people's patches. If you started showing up in week 4 as the plan specifies, you already know which maintainer reviews what and which issues are genuinely open rather than stale. If you did not, ship the smallest correct fix you can find and accept that this is a week-51 acquaintance, not a week-51 reputation.

items.title: Pick the repo by who reads it, not by issue count
items.desc: inspect_ai is built by UK AISI and its contributor list is read by people who hire evals engineers. lm-evaluation-harness is EleutherAI's and has a documented path for adding a new task. verifiers is Prime Intellect's and sits directly under the Environments Hub. Choose one and go deep; three shallow PRs across three repos read as tourism.

items.title: Publish the environment to the Environments Hub
items.desc: Package it against the verifiers interface and publish it publicly with the variance numbers in the description. This is the lowest-contested, highest-signal placement available to you: it is a real registry, people install from it, and it is where teams at Prime Intellect and elsewhere go looking for environment builders. Watch for install failures after publishing and fix them the same week.

callouts.html: A merge is not under your control; a clean PR is. Reviewer latency on major repos runs weeks. A substantive, tested, in-review PR is portfolio evidence — link it as such and do not stall the rest of Phase 4 waiting on a maintainer.

items.title: Audit the funnel you opened in week 20
items.desc: You have been applying for 32 weeks. Pull the list: what you sent, to whom, what came back, where it died. Cold email with no referral converts at approximately zero, so if that is most of your list the problem is channel, not résumé. Count how many applications went through a person who already knew your work versus a careers form, and fix the ratio.

items.title: Structured programs are the real funnel
items.desc: Fixed windows, published criteria, and they hire people at exactly your level. ARENA and MATS run on dated cohorts; the Anthropic Fellows programme takes roughly 32 people per cohort, about 21% of finalists, and 25–50% convert to full-time. Apply to every window that falls inside or just after your 52 weeks, including the ones you feel unready for — the selection rate on programs you did not apply to is zero.

items.title: Apply to the adjacent employers who hire at this level
items.desc: Frontier labs are not the only buyers of this skill set and are the hardest first step. UK AISI builds Inspect and hires straight from contributions to it; US CAISI, METR, Apollo Research, Redwood Research, EpochAI, Ai2, EleutherAI, Prime Intellect and LMArena all staff evals and environments work, as do the eval-data vendors. Several of them recruit directly from open-source contributor lists, which is why Task 03 comes before this one.

items.title: Send the version that leads with reliability
items.desc: Same portfolio link every time, different first paragraph. Lead with the environment, its measured variance, and the stranger who installed it; then the benchmark audit and the discrepancy you reported. Name the specific team and the specific thing they published that your work touches. If you cannot write that sentence for a role, you are not a fit for it yet and the application is noise.

callouts.html: The honest framing for week 52. You are a credible candidate for evals and environments roles at safety orgs, eval vendors and applied teams. Frontier-lab applied research is a 2–4 year path that usually routes through one of those, or through a fellowship. Apply accordingly and stop treating a lab offer as the only pass condition.

milestone.title: The portfolio
milestone.heading: One link. Three flagship artifacts above the fold, then the supporting work.
items: SHIP: A published environment — task, verifier, reset, reward — with measured run-to-run variance, stated reliability, and a stranger who installed it and got a result
SHIP: A benchmark protocol-compliance audit: a published agentic result reproduced, the discrepancy found, documented, and reported to the authors
SHIP: One repo carrying CS336 assignment 1 green against the course test suite plus your nanochat speedrun writeup with real costs and honest variance
SHIP: A technical report as a linkable web page, a README that answers what/how/how-reliable on the first screen, and one blog post with a defensible claim backed by your own numbers
SHIP: A substantive public contribution to inspect_ai, lm-evaluation-harness or verifiers — merged, or in review and clean — plus the environment live on the Environments Hub
SHIP: An application record covering 32 weeks: every structured-program window inside the 52 weeks applied to, and adjacent employers approached through contributions rather than careers forms
SHIP: You can state your environment's variance, its dominant noise source, and what you would need to halve it — without checking your notes

overview.h1_line1: From weak Python to a published
overview.intro: A 52-week plan at 25 hours per week — about 1,300 hours — that ends with work a hiring manager can install and run. It assumes you are starting close to zero and takes you through Python, deep learning and transformers, distributed systems and scaling, then evals, RL and environments. Everything is public from week 1, and applications start at week 20, not week 52.
overview.honesty: What 1,300 hours actually buys. Fifty-two weeks at this intensity makes you a credible candidate for evals and environments roles at safety orgs, eval vendors and applied teams. Frontier-lab applied research is a 2–4 year path, and it usually routes through one of those roles or through a fellowship. This plan is the first leg, honestly labelled.
overview.budget: Total cost: $700–2,500. That covers the nanochat speedrun ($150–400 on rented 8×H100), fine-tuning and RL runs, and — the line the old plan omitted entirely — the API cost of eval baselines. Baselines are not one pass: a variance estimate needs five runs of every sample across every model you compare, and that is where the bill lands. Set a hard cap per experiment before you start and never leave an instance running overnight.
